query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, a small, controlled addition of a carefully chosen alloying element (e.g., ~2 at.% Ti) will shift the phase equilibrium toward a single disordered solid solution (FCC or BCC) by suppressing the formation of brittle, coarse intermetallic compounds. This altered phase balance is responsible for simultaneously maintaining high-temperature strength, environmental and radiation resistance, and cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: The baseline Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy without the added element typically exhibits mixed phase(s) (a combination of disordered solid solution and minor intermetallic phases) that limit its overall performance balance.
generation.intervention: Introduce a small percentage (approximately 2 at.%) of an element like Ti via controlled compositional tuning.
generation.conditions: Processing under identical thermal histories and testing conditions (e.g., identical annealing and cooling protocols) for both the baseline and modified alloy; mechanical and environmental testing across high-temperature, radiation-exposure, and cryogenic conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The emergence of a predominantly disordered solid solution (FCC or BCC), with reduced intermetallic formation, mediates the improvement in the multi-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.mechanism: The added alloying element (Ti) creates local lattice strain and affects atomic size mismatch, which suppresses nucleation and growth of brittle intermetallic phases and stabilizes the disordered phase. In doing so, it preserves high-temperature strength and simultaneously enables the alloy to resist environmental degradation, radiation-induced defects, and maintain toughness at cryogenic temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Ti-modified alloy will exhibit a higher fraction (e.g., >80% compared to <70% in the baseline) of the stable disordered phase along with statistically significant improvements in high-temperature strength, radiation tolerance, environmental resistance, and cryogenic toughness relative to the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy without the Ti addition under the same heat treatment and testing conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is limited to the specified compositional range (minor alloying additions around 2 at.%) and the processing conditions used. Exceeding this range or differing thermal histories may lead to alternative phase stability and are beyond the current scope.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative change in phase fractions and property metrics remains uncertain without experimental confirmation. Further variation in the nature and amount of the alloying element might yield different outcomes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the baseline Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy and another set with a 2 at.% addition of Ti. Subject both sets to identical processing (annealing/cooling) and testing protocols that include phase analysis, high-temperature mechanical testing, radiation exposure tests, and cryogenic toughness measurements.
measurements: Phase analysis via X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to quantify phase fractions.
Mechanical property tests (e.g., hardness, tensile tests) at high temperatures and cryogenic temperatures.
Radiation exposure tests to assess defect tolerance.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-modified alloy does not show a statistically significant increase in disordered phase fraction and associated improvements in mechanical and environmental performance compared to the baseline, the hypothesis that controlled Ti addition governs phase stability and the desirable property combination is falsified.

chosen.approach: Compositional tuning via element addition in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs
